slides.headline: Seven small habits that make the tools actually work
slides.sub: None of them is clever. All seven are the difference between an answer you rewrite and one you send.

slides.text: attach the real file, not a description of it
slides.note: The tidied version you paste in is already an interpretation. Give it the messy original and the mess becomes information.

slides.text: name the reader before you name the task
slides.note: "For a finance director with five minutes" changes the answer more than any clever wording you can add afterwards.

slides.text: say what to do when the answer is not in there
slides.note: Ask it to write [GAP] or [CHECK] where your notes run out. Asked to mark its guesses, it marks them.

slides.text: ask for the questions, not the summary
slides.note: A summary tells you what a document says. Ten hard questions tell you what it costs you. Only one of those is worth ten minutes.

slides.text: say out loud that the numbers must not move
slides.note: Keep every figure and date exactly as written. It is one sentence and it removes the failure that matters most.

slides.text: hand it the template you already use
slides.note: Your own headings, your own order. Starting from your structure beats any first draft written from nothing.

slides.text: read the first answer as a draft, not a verdict
slides.note: The second attempt is where the work is. People who get nothing out of these tools almost always stopped after one.

slides.headline: Twenty-five prompts, written out in full
slides.body: Each one gives the task in plain words, the prompt itself, what to attach, and what a good answer looks like. Free, no email, no form.
slides.foot: Written for UK teams. None of them needs personal data to work; where a task touches people, the prompt asks for roles and situations, not names.
